title: VII. The First And Rightful Lover
paragraphs: With his long, quick strides, Mitya walked straight up to the table.

"Gentlemen," he said, in a loud voice, almost shouting, yet stammering at every word, "I ... I'm all right! Don't be afraid!" he exclaimed. "I — there's nothing wrong," he said, turning suddenly to Grushenka, who had shrunk back in her chair toward Kalganov and gripped his hand tight. "I ... I'm coming too. I'm here till morning. Gentlemen, may I stay with you till morning? Just till morning, for the last time, in this same room?"
That's how he finished, turning to the fat little man with the pipe, seated on the sofa. The man removed his pipe from his lips with dignity and observed severely:
"Panie, this is a private gathering. There are other rooms."
"Why, it's you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch! What do you mean by this?" Kalganov answered suddenly. "Sit down with us. How are you?"
"Delighted to see you, my dear ... precious fellow, I've always thought highly of you," Mitya responded, joyfully and eagerly, at once reaching his hand across the table.
"Aie! What a grip! You've nearly broken my fingers," laughed Kalganov.

"He always squeezes like that, always," Grushenka put in cheerfully, with a timid smile, seeming suddenly convinced from Mitya's face that he wasn't going to make a scene. She was watching him with intense curiosity and still some unease. Something about him struck her, and indeed the last thing she'd expected was for him to walk in and speak like this, at a moment like this.
"Good evening," Maximov ventured mildly, on the left. Mitya rushed over to him too.

"Good evening. You're here too! How glad I am to find you here as well! Gentlemen, gentlemen, I—" (he addressed the Polish gentleman with the pipe again, clearly taking him for the most important person present) "—I flew here.... I wanted to spend my last day, my last hour, in this room, this very room ... where I too once worshipped ... my queen.... Forgive me, panie," he cried wildly, "I flew here and swore an oath — Oh, don't be afraid, it's my last night! Let's drink to our good understanding. They'll bring the wine directly.... I brought this with me." (Something made him pull out his bundle of notes.) "Allow me, panie! I want music, singing, a proper revel, like we had before. But the worm, the unneeded worm, will crawl off, and there'll be no more of him. I'll mark my day of joy on my last night."

He was nearly choking. There was so much, so much he wanted to say, but only strange exclamations made it out of his mouth. The Pole stared fixedly at him, at the bundle of notes in his hand, glanced at Grushenka, and was plainly puzzled.
"If my sovereign lady will permit—" he began.

"What does 'sovereign' mean? I suppose it means 'sovereign'?" Grushenka broke in. "I can't help laughing at you, the way you talk. Sit down, Mitya, what are you going on about? Don't frighten us, please. You won't frighten us, will you? If you won't, I'm glad to see you ..."
"Me, frighten you?" cried Mitya, flinging up his hands. "Oh, pass me by, go your way, I won't stand in it!..."

And suddenly he surprised everyone, and no doubt himself as well, by dropping into a chair and bursting into tears, turning his head away toward the far wall, his arms clasped tight around the chair back as though embracing it.

"Now, now, what a fellow you are!" Grushenka cried, reproachfully. "That's exactly how he comes to see me — he starts talking, and I can't make out a word of it. He cried like that once before, and now he's crying again! It's shameful! Why are you crying? As if you had anything to cry about!" she added, cryptically, stressing each word with a touch of irritation.
"I ... I'm not crying.... Well, good evening!" He spun round in his chair at once, and suddenly laughed — not his abrupt, wooden laugh, but a long, quivering, near-silent, nervous laugh.

"Well, there you go again.... Come, cheer up, cheer up!" Grushenka coaxed him. "I'm very glad you've come, very glad, Mitya, do you hear — very glad! I want him to stay here with us," she said, peremptorily, addressing the whole company, though her words were plainly meant for the man on the sofa. "I want it, I want it! And if he goes, I go too!" she added, her eyes flashing.
"Whatever my queen commands is law!" the Pole pronounced, gallantly kissing Grushenka's hand. "I invite you, panie, to join our company," he added politely, to Mitya.
Mitya was on his feet, clearly meaning to launch into another speech, but the words wouldn't come.
"Let's drink, panie," he blurted instead of making a speech. Everyone laughed.

"Good heavens! I thought he was about to start up again!" Grushenka exclaimed, nervously. "Do you hear, Mitya," she went on, insistently, "don't go prancing about, but it's nice you brought the champagne. I want some myself, I can't stand liqueurs. And best of all, you've come yourself. We were terribly bored here.... You've come for another spree, I suppose? But put your money away. Where did you get so much?"

All this while Mitya had been holding the crumpled bundle of notes in his hand, and every eye in the room, especially the Poles', was fixed on it. Embarrassed, he shoved it hastily into his pocket. He flushed. At that moment the innkeeper brought in an uncorked bottle of champagne and glasses on a tray. Mitya grabbed the bottle, but was so flustered he had no idea what to do with it. Kalganov took it from him and poured the champagne.

"Another! Another bottle!" Mitya called to the innkeeper, and, forgetting to clink glasses with the Pole he'd so solemnly invited to drink to their good understanding, drank off his glass without waiting for anyone else. His whole face suddenly changed. The solemn, tragic look he'd walked in with vanished completely, replaced by something childlike. He seemed to have turned gentle and subdued all at once. He looked around at everyone shyly and happily, with a constant nervous little laugh, wearing the blissful look of a dog who's misbehaved, been punished, and been forgiven. He seemed to have forgotten everything, gazing round at everyone with a childlike, delighted smile. He looked at Grushenka, laughing continually, and pulled his chair close to hers. By degrees he formed some impression of the two Poles, though nothing definite yet.

The Pole on the sofa struck him with his dignified manner and his Polish accent, and above all with his pipe. "Well, what of it? It's good that he smokes a pipe," he mused. The Pole's puffy, middle-aged face, with its tiny nose and two very thin, pointed, dyed, insolent-looking mustaches, hadn't yet raised the faintest doubt in Mitya's mind. He wasn't even particularly struck by the Pole's absurd Siberian-made wig, with its foolish little curls combed forward at the temples. "I suppose it's all fine, since he wears a wig," he went on, musing blissfully. The other, younger Pole, staring insolently and defiantly at the company and listening to the conversation with silent contempt, impressed Mitya only by his great height, so strikingly different from the Pole on the sofa. "If he stood up, he'd be six foot three." The thought flitted through Mitya's mind. It occurred to him too that this Pole must be the other one's friend, a kind of "bodyguard," and no doubt the big Pole was at the disposal of the little one with the pipe. But all this seemed to Mitya perfectly natural and not worth questioning. In his dog-like mood of submission, every trace of rivalry had died away.

Grushenka's mood, and the cryptic tone of some of her remarks, he utterly failed to grasp. All he understood, with a thrill in his heart, was that she was being kind to him, that she'd forgiven him, and had made him sit beside her. He was beside himself with delight, watching her sip her glass of champagne. The silence of the company seemed to strike him somehow, though, and he glanced round at everyone with expectant eyes.
"Why are we just sitting here, gentlemen? Why don't we get on with something?" his smiling eyes seemed to ask.
"He keeps talking nonsense, and we were all laughing," Kalganov said suddenly, as though reading his mind, pointing at Maximov.
Mitya at once stared at Kalganov, and then at Maximov.
"He's talking nonsense?" he laughed, his short, wooden laugh, seeming suddenly delighted at something — "ha ha!"
"Yes. Would you believe it, he insists that in the eighteen-twenties all our cavalry officers married Polish women. That's absolute rot, isn't it?"
"Polish women?" Mitya repeated, in perfect ecstasy.

Kalganov was well aware of Mitya's feelings for Grushenka, and had guessed about the Pole too, but that interested him only slightly, perhaps not at all; what interested him was Maximov. He'd come here with Maximov by chance, and had met the Poles at the inn for the first time in his life just now. He'd known Grushenka before, and had once called on her with someone; but she hadn't taken to him. Yet tonight she looked at him very warmly: before Mitya's arrival she'd been making much of him, though he seemed somehow unmoved by it. He was a boy, not yet twenty, dressed like a dandy, with a charming, fair-skinned face and splendid thick fair hair. From that fair face looked out beautiful pale blue eyes, with an intelligent, sometimes even deep expression, well beyond his years — though the young man sometimes looked and talked quite like a child, and wasn't at all ashamed of it, even when he noticed it himself. As a rule he was very willful, even capricious, though always friendly. Sometimes there was something fixed, obstinate, in his expression. He'd look at you and listen, seeming all the while to be lost in some private daydream. Often he was listless and lazy; at other times he'd grow excited, sometimes, it seemed, over the most trivial things.

"Just imagine, I've been dragging him around with me for the last four days," he went on, drawling his words lazily, though quite naturally, without the slightest affectation. "Ever since your brother — remember? — shoved him off the carriage and sent him flying. That's what got me interested in him at the time, and I took him out to the country, but he keeps talking such rot I'm ashamed to be seen with him. I'm taking him back."
"The gentleman has never seen Polish ladies, and says what's impossible," the Pole with the pipe observed to Maximov.
He spoke Russian fairly well, at any rate far better than he let on. Whenever he used a Russian word, he always twisted it into a Polish shape.
"But I was married to a Polish lady myself," Maximov tittered.
"But did you serve in the cavalry? You were talking about the cavalry. Were you a cavalry officer?" Kalganov put in at once.
"Was he a cavalry officer, indeed! Ha ha!" cried Mitya, listening eagerly, turning his inquiring eyes from one to another as though there were no telling what he might hear from each.

"No, you see," Maximov turned to him. "What I mean is, those pretty Polish ladies ... when they danced the mazurka with our Uhlans ... when one of them dances a mazurka with a Uhlan, she jumps onto his knee like a kitten ... a little white one ... and the pan-father and pan-mother look on and allow it.... They allow it ... and the next day the Uhlan comes and offers her his hand.... That's how it is ... offers her his hand, he he!" Maximov finished, tittering.

"The pan is a lajdak!" the tall Pole on the chair suddenly growled, crossing one leg over the other. Mitya's eye caught his huge, greased boot with its thick, dirty sole. Both Poles' clothing looked rather greasy.
"Now it's 'lajdak'! What's he scolding about?" said Grushenka, suddenly vexed.
"Pani Agrippina, what the gentleman saw in Poland were servant girls, not ladies of good family," the Pole with the pipe observed to Grushenka.
"You may depend on that," the tall Pole snapped, contemptuously.
"What next! Let him talk! People talk — why stop them? It makes things livelier," Grushenka said, crossly.
"I'm not stopping anyone, pani," said the Pole in the wig, with a long look at Grushenka, and, lapsing back into dignified silence, sucked at his pipe again.

"No, no. The Polish gentleman is telling the truth." Kalganov grew excited again, as though it were a matter of vast importance. "He's never been to Poland, so how can he talk about it? You weren't married in Poland, were you?"

"No, in the province of Smolensk. Only, a Uhlan had brought her to Russia before that — my future wife — along with her mother, her aunt, and another female relation with a grown son. He brought her straight from Poland and handed her over to me. He was a lieutenant in our regiment, a very nice young man. At first he meant to marry her himself. But he didn't, because it turned out she was lame."
"So you married a lame woman?" cried Kalganov.
"Yes. They both deceived me a little at the time, and hid it from me. I thought she was hopping; she kept hopping.... I thought it was for fun."
"So pleased she was, to be marrying you!" Kalganov shrieked, in a ringing, childish voice.

"Yes, so pleased. But it turned out to be for quite a different reason. Later, once we were married, that very evening after the wedding, she confessed, and very touchingly asked my forgiveness. 'I jumped over a puddle once, as a child,' she said, 'and hurt my leg.' He he!"
Kalganov burst into the most childish laughter, nearly falling onto the sofa. Grushenka laughed too. Mitya was at the height of happiness.

"You know, that's actually true — he's not lying this time," Kalganov exclaimed, turning to Mitya. "And you know, he's been married twice — that's his first wife he's talking about. But his second wife, you know, ran off, and she's still alive."
"Is that possible?" said Mitya, turning quickly to Maximov with an expression of utter astonishment.

"Yes. She ran off, all right. I've had that unpleasant experience," Maximov admitted modestly, "with a monsieur. And worse still, she'd had all my little property signed over to her beforehand. 'You're an educated man,' she told me. 'You can always earn a living.' That's how she settled the matter. A venerable bishop once told me: 'One of your wives was lame, but the other was too light on her feet.' He he!"

"Listen, listen!" cried Kalganov, bubbling over. "If he's lying — and he often is — he's only doing it to entertain us all. There's no harm in that, is there? You know, I actually like him sometimes. He's awfully low, but it's natural to him, isn't it? Don't you think so? Some people are low out of self-interest, but he's simply low by nature. Just imagine, he claims — he was arguing about it the whole way yesterday — that Gogol wrote Dead Souls about him. You remember, there's a landowner named Maximov in it, whom Nozdryov thrashes. He was charged, remember, 'with inflicting bodily injury by rods on the landowner Maximov while in a state of intoxication.' Would you believe it, he claims he was that Maximov, and that he was the one beaten! Now, can that be so? Tchitchikov made his journey, at the very latest, in the early eighteen-twenties, so the dates don't add up. He couldn't have been beaten then — could he?"
It was hard to say what exactly had Kalganov so worked up, but his excitement was genuine. Mitya followed his lead without objection.
"Well, but what if they did thrash him!" he cried, laughing.
"It's not exactly that they thrashed me, but what I mean is—" Maximov put in.
"What do you mean? Either they thrashed you or they didn't."
"What time is it, panie?" the Pole with the pipe asked his tall friend, with a bored air. The other shrugged in reply. Neither of them owned a watch.

"Why shouldn't he talk? Let other people talk. Must other people go quiet just because you're bored?" Grushenka flew at him, plainly out to pick a fight. For the first time something seemed to flash across Mitya's mind. This time the Pole answered with unmistakable irritation.
"Pani, I raised no objection. I said nothing."
"All right, then. Come, tell us your story," Grushenka called to Maximov. "Why's everyone gone silent?"

"There's nothing to tell, it's all so foolish," Maximov answered at once, with evident satisfaction, mincing a little. "Besides, it's all allegory in Gogol, since he gave every name a hidden meaning. Nozdryov's real name was Nosov, and Kuvshinikov had an entirely different name — he was called Shkvornev. Fenardi really was called Fenardi, only he wasn't Italian, he was Russian, and Mamzelle Fenardi was a pretty girl with pretty little legs in tights, and a little short skirt with spangles, and she'd spin round and round, only not for four hours, just four minutes, and she bewitched everyone..."
"But what were you beaten for?" cried Kalganov.
"For Piron!" Maximov answered.
"What Piron?" cried Mitya.

"The famous French writer, Piron. We were all drinking then, a big party of us, at a tavern at that very fair. They'd invited me, and I started off by quoting epigrams. 'Is that you, Boileau? What a ridiculous get-up!' And Boileau answers that he's off to a masquerade — that is, to the baths, he he! And they took it as aimed at them, so I hurried to recite another, a very biting one, known to every educated person:
Yes, Sappho and Phaon are we! But one grief weighs upon me. You don't know your way to the sea!

They took even more offense, and began abusing me in the most unseemly way for it. And, wouldn't you know it, trying to set things right, I launched into a very refined anecdote about Piron — how he wasn't accepted into the French Academy, and, to get his revenge, wrote his own epitaph:
Ci-gît Piron qui ne fut rien, Pas même académicien.
They grabbed me and thrashed me."
"But what for? What for?"
"For my education. People can thrash a man for anything," Maximov concluded, briefly and sententiously.
"Eh, that's enough! It's all stupid, I don't want to hear it. I thought it would be amusing," Grushenka cut them off, suddenly.

Mitya started, and at once stopped laughing. The tall Pole rose to his feet and, with the haughty air of a man bored and out of his element, began pacing from corner to corner of the room, his hands behind his back.
"Ah, he can't sit still," said Grushenka, eyeing him with contempt. Mitya began to feel uneasy. He noticed, besides, that the Pole on the sofa was watching him with an irritated expression.
"Panie!" cried Mitya, "let's drink! And the other pan too! Let's drink."
In a flash he'd pulled three glasses toward him and filled them with champagne.
"To Poland, panovie, I drink to your Poland!" cried Mitya.
"I shall be delighted, panie," said the Pole on the sofa, with dignity and gracious condescension, and took his glass.
"And the other pan, what's his name? Drink, most illustrious, take your glass!" Mitya urged.
"Pan Vrublevsky," the Pole on the sofa supplied.
Pan Vrublevsky came up to the table, swaying as he walked.
"To Poland, panovie!" cried Mitya, raising his glass. "Hurrah!"
All three drank. Mitya seized the bottle and poured three more glasses.
"Now to Russia, panovie, and let's be brothers!"
"Pour some for us," said Grushenka. "I'll drink to Russia too!"
"So will I," said Kalganov.
"And I would too ... to Russia, the old grandmother!" Maximov tittered.
"All of you! All of you!" cried Mitya. "Trifon Borissovitch, more bottles!"
The other three bottles Mitya had brought were set on the table. Mitya filled the glasses.
"To Russia! Hurrah!" he shouted again. Everyone drank the toast except the Poles, and Grushenka drained her whole glass at once. The Poles didn't touch theirs.
"How's this, panovie?" cried Mitya. "Won't you drink it?"
Pan Vrublevsky took his glass, raised it, and said in a resonant voice:
"To Russia, as she was before 1772."
"There, that's better!" cried the other Pole, and both drained their glasses at once.
"You're fools, you panovie," burst out of Mitya suddenly.
"Panie!" both Poles shouted menacingly, squaring up at Mitya like a pair of fighting cocks. Pan Vrublevsky was especially furious.
"Can a man help loving his own country?" he shouted.

"Quiet! No quarreling! I won't have any quarreling!" Grushenka cried imperiously, stamping her foot on the floor. Her face glowed, her eyes shone. The effects of the glass she'd just drunk were plain to see. Mitya was terribly alarmed.
"Panovie, forgive me! It was my fault, I'm sorry. Vrublevsky, panie Vrublevsky, I'm sorry."
"Hold your tongue, you, at least! Sit down, you fool!" Grushenka scolded, in angry annoyance.
Everyone sat down. All fell silent, looking at one another.
"Gentlemen, it was all my fault," Mitya began again, unable to make sense of Grushenka's words. "Come, why are we just sitting here? What shall we do ... to amuse ourselves again?"
"Ach, it's certainly anything but amusing!" Kalganov mumbled lazily.
"Let's play faro again, like we were doing before," Maximov suddenly tittered.
"Faro? Splendid!" cried Mitya. "If only the panovie—"
"It's lite, panovie," the Pole on the sofa responded, as if reluctantly.
"That's true," Pan Vrublevsky agreed.
"Lite? What do you mean, 'lite'?" asked Grushenka.
"Late, pani! I mean, 'a late hour,'" the Pole on the sofa explained.

"It's always late with them. They can never manage anything!" Grushenka nearly shrieked in her anger. "They're bored themselves, so they want everyone else bored too. Before you came, Mitya, they were sitting just as silent, turning up their noses at me."
"My goddess!" cried the Pole on the sofa. "I see you're not well-disposed toward me — that's why I'm gloomy. I'm ready, panie," he added, addressing Mitya.
"Begin, panie," Mitya agreed, pulling his notes from his pocket and laying two hundred-rouble notes on the table. "I want to lose a lot to you. Take the cards. Bank it."
"We'll get cards from the landlord, panie," said the little Pole, gravely and firmly.
"That's much the best way," Pan Vrublevsky chimed in.
"From the landlord? Very good, I understand, let's get them from him. Cards!" Mitya shouted at the landlord.

The landlord brought in a new, unopened pack, and informed Mitya that the girls were getting ready, and that the Jews with the cymbals would very likely be along soon, but the cart with the provisions hadn't arrived yet. Mitya jumped up from the table and ran into the next room to give orders, but only three girls had arrived so far, and Marya wasn't among them yet. He didn't quite know himself what orders to give, or why he'd run out at all. He only told them to take the presents for the girls out of the box — the sweets, the toffee, the fondants. "And vodka for Andrey, vodka for Andrey!" he cried hurriedly. "I was rude to Andrey!"
Suddenly Maximov, who'd followed him out, touched him on the shoulder.
"Give me five roubles," he whispered to Mitya. "I'll stake something at faro too, he he!"
"Splendid! Capital! Take ten, here!"
Again he pulled all the notes out of his pocket and picked out a ten-rouble one. "And if you lose that, come back, come back again."

"Very good," Maximov whispered joyfully, and ran back inside. Mitya returned too, apologizing for keeping them waiting. The Poles had already sat down and opened the pack. They looked much more amiable now, almost cordial. The Pole on the sofa had lit another pipe and was preparing to deal. He wore an air of solemnity.
"To your places, gentlemen," cried Pan Vrublevsky.
"No, I'm not playing anymore," Kalganov remarked. "I've already lost fifty roubles to them just now."
"The pan had no luck — perhaps he'll be lucky this time," the Pole on the sofa observed, in his direction.
"How much in the bank? To match?" asked Mitya.
"That depends, panie — maybe a hundred, maybe two hundred, as much as you care to stake."
"A million!" laughed Mitya.
"Has the Pan Captain perhaps heard of Pan Podvysotsky?"
"What Podvysotsky?"

"In Warsaw there was a bank, and anyone could come stake against it. Podvysotsky comes, sees a thousand gold pieces, stakes against the bank. The banker says, 'Panie Podvysotsky, are you laying down the gold, or must we trust to your honor?' 'To my honor, panie,' says Podvysotsky. 'So much the better.' The banker throws the dice. Podvysotsky wins. 'Take it, panie,' says the banker, and, pulling out the drawer, hands him a million. 'Take it, panie, it's your winnings.' There was a million in the bank. 'I didn't know that,' says Podvysotsky. 'Panie Podvysotsky,' says the banker, 'you pledged your honor, and we pledged ours.' Podvysotsky took the million."
"That's not true," said Kalganov.
"Panie Kalganov, in gentlemanly company one doesn't say such things."

"As if a Polish gambler would ever give away a million!" cried Mitya, but checked himself at once. "Forgive me, panie, my fault again — he would, he would give away a million, for honor, for Polish honor. See how I speak Polish, ha ha! Here, I stake ten roubles, the jack leads."

"And I'll put a rouble on the queen, the queen of hearts, the pretty little panienotchka, he he!" laughed Maximov, drawing out his queen, and, as though trying to hide it from everyone, leaned in close and hurriedly crossed himself under the table. Mitya won. The rouble won too.
"A corner!" cried Mitya.
"I'll bet another rouble, a 'single' stake," Maximov muttered gleefully, thoroughly delighted at having won a rouble.
"Lost!" shouted Mitya. "A 'double' on the seven!"
The seven was trumped too.
"Stop!" Kalganov cried suddenly.
"Double! Double!" Mitya doubled his stakes, and every time he doubled, the Poles trumped the card he'd doubled. The rouble stakes kept winning.
"On the double!" Mitya shouted furiously.
"You've lost two hundred, panie. Will you stake another hundred?" the Pole on the sofa asked.
"What? Lost two hundred already? Then another two hundred! All doubles!"
And pulling his money out of his pocket, Mitya was about to throw two hundred roubles on the queen, but Kalganov covered it with his hand.
"That's enough!" he shouted, in his ringing voice.
"What's the matter?" Mitya stared at him.
"That's enough! I don't want you playing anymore. Don't!"
"Why not?"
"Because I don't want you to. Hang it, come away. That's why. I won't let you keep playing."
Mitya gazed at him in astonishment.
"Give it up, Mitya. He may be right. You've lost a lot as it is," said Grushenka, with a strange note in her voice. Both Poles rose from their seats, looking deeply offended.
"Are you joking, panie?" said the short one, staring severely at Kalganov.
"How dare you!" Pan Vrublevsky growled at Kalganov too.
"Don't you dare shout like that," cried Grushenka. "Ah, you turkey-cocks!"
Mitya looked at each of them in turn. But something in Grushenka's face suddenly struck him, and in that same instant something new flashed into his mind — a strange, new thought!
"Pani Agrippina," the little Pole was beginning, crimson with anger, when Mitya suddenly walked up to him and slapped him on the shoulder.
"Most illustrious, a word with you."
"What do you want?"
"In the next room — I have two words to say to you, something pleasant, very pleasant. You'll be glad to hear it."
The little pan was taken aback, and eyed Mitya apprehensively. He agreed at once, all the same, on condition that Pan Vrublevsky came along too.
"The bodyguard? Let him come — I want him along too. I need him!" cried Mitya. "March, panovie!"
"Where are you going?" Grushenka asked anxiously.
"We'll be back in a moment," Mitya answered.
There was a kind of boldness, a sudden confidence, shining in his eyes now. His face had looked very different an hour before, when he'd first walked into the room.

He led the Poles not into the large room where the girls' chorus was gathering and the table was being laid, but into the bedroom on the right, where the trunks and bundles were kept, with two large beds and pyramids of cotton pillows on each. A lit candle stood on a small deal table in the corner. The little man and Mitya sat down at this table, facing each other, while the huge Vrublevsky stood beside them, hands behind his back. The Poles looked severe but were plainly curious.
"What can I do for you, panie?" the little Pole lisped.
"Well, look here, panie, I won't keep you long. There's money here for you," he pulled out his notes. "Would you like three thousand? Take it and be on your way."
The Pole stared wide-eyed at Mitya, searchingly.
"Three thousand, panie?" He exchanged glances with Vrublevsky.

"Three, panovie, three! Listen, panie, I can see you're a sensible man. Take three thousand and go to the devil, and Vrublevsky with you — d'you hear? But at once, this very minute, and forever. You understand me, panie — forever. There's the door, you go through it. What have you got there, a greatcoat, a fur coat? I'll bring it out to you. They'll have the horses out directly, and then — goodbye, panie!"
Mitya waited for an answer with confidence. He had no doubts. A look of extraordinary resolve crossed the Pole's face.
"And the money, panie?"

"The money, panie? Five hundred roubles I'll give you this instant, for the journey and as a first installment, and two thousand five hundred tomorrow, in town — I swear on my honor, I'll get it, I'll get it whatever it costs!" cried Mitya.
The Poles exchanged glances again. The short man's face darkened further.

"Seven hundred, seven hundred, not five hundred, right now, this minute, cash in hand!" Mitya added, sensing something was wrong. "What's the matter, panie? Don't you trust me? I can't hand over the full three thousand straight off. If I did, you might just come back to her tomorrow.... Besides, I don't have the three thousand on me. It's at home, in town," Mitya faltered, his spirits sinking with every word. "On my word, the money's there, hidden away."
Instantly, an extraordinary air of personal dignity came over the little man's face.
"What next?" he asked, ironically. "For shame!" And he spat on the floor. Pan Vrublevsky spat too.
"You do that, panie," said Mitya, realizing with despair that it was all over, "because you're hoping to squeeze more out of Grushenka? A pair of capons, that's what you are!"

"This is a mortal insult!" The little Pole flushed crab-red, and strode out of the room, briskly, as if unwilling to hear another word. Vrublevsky swung out after him, and Mitya followed, embarrassed and crestfallen. He was afraid of Grushenka, afraid the pan would immediately raise an outcry. And that's exactly what he did. The Pole walked into the room and flung himself before Grushenka in a theatrical pose.
"Pani Agrippina, I have received a mortal insult!" he exclaimed. But Grushenka suddenly lost all patience, as though they'd wounded her in the most tender spot.
"Speak Russian! Speak Russian!" she cried. "Not another word of Polish! You used to speak Russian. You can't have forgotten it in five years."
She was red with fury.
"Pani Agrippina—"
"My name's Agrafena, Grushenka — speak Russian, or I won't listen!"
The Pole gasped with offended dignity, and delivered himself, quickly and pompously, in broken Russian:
"Pani Agrafena, I came here to forget the past and forgive it, to forget everything that's happened up till today—"
"Forgive? Came here to forgive me?" Grushenka cut him off, jumping up from her seat.
"Just so, pani, I'm no coward, I'm magnanimous. But I was astounded when I saw your lovers. Pan Mitya offered me three thousand, in the other room, to leave. I spat in the pan's face."
"What? He offered you money for me?" cried Grushenka, hysterically. "Is that true, Mitya? How dare you? Am I for sale?"
"Panie, panie!" Mitya shouted, "she's pure and radiant, and I've never been her lover! That's a lie...."

"How dare you defend me to him?" Grushenka shrieked. "It wasn't virtue that kept me pure, and it wasn't that I was afraid of Kuzma — it was so that I could hold my head up when I met him and tell him he's a scoundrel. And did he really turn down the money?"
"He took it! He took it!" cried Mitya. "Only he wanted the full three thousand at once, and I could only give him seven hundred outright."
"I see — he heard I had money, and came here to marry me!"
"Pani Agrippina!" cried the little Pole. "I'm — a knight, I'm — a nobleman, not a lajdak. I came here to make you my wife, and I find you a different woman — perverse and shameless."

"Oh, go back where you came from! I'll have them throw you out, and out you'll go," cried Grushenka, furiously. "I've been a fool, a fool, to have made myself miserable these five years! And it wasn't for his sake — it was my own anger that made me miserable. And this isn't even him at all! Was he like this? He could be his own father! Where did you get that wig? He was a falcon, and this is a gander. He used to laugh and sing to me.... And I've been crying for five years — a damned fool, abject, shameless I was!"
She sank back into her low chair and buried her face in her hands. At that instant the Mokroe chorus struck up in the room to the left — a rollicking dance song.
"A regular Sodom!" Vrublevsky suddenly roared. "Landlord, send the shameless hussies away!"
The landlord, who'd been peeping curiously in at the door for some time, hearing the shouting and guessing his guests were quarreling, stepped in at once.
"What are you shouting for? Trying to split your throat?" he said to Vrublevsky, with startling rudeness.
"Animal!" bellowed Pan Vrublevsky.

"Animal, is it? And what sort of cards were you playing with just now? I gave you a fresh pack and you hid it. You were playing with marked cards! I could send you to Siberia for playing with false cards, d'you know that — it's the same as forging banknotes...."
And going up to the sofa, he thrust his fingers between the sofa back and the cushion, and pulled out an unopened pack of cards.
"Here's my pack, still unopened!"
He held it up for the whole room to see. "From where I was standing I saw him slip my pack away and put his own in its place — you're a cheat, not a gentleman!"
"And I saw the pan switch a card, twice!" cried Kalganov.
"How shameful! How shameful!" Grushenka exclaimed, clasping her hands, blushing with genuine shame. "Good Lord, has he come to this?"
"I thought as much myself!" said Mitya. But before he'd finished saying it, Vrublevsky, his face confused and furious, shook his fist at Grushenka, shouting:
"You low harlot!"
Mitya flew at him at once, seized him with both hands, lifted him bodily into the air, and in an instant had carried him into the room on the right, the one they'd just come from.
"I've laid him out on the floor in there," he announced, coming back at once, gasping with excitement. "He's struggling, the scoundrel! But he won't be coming back, no fear of that!..."
He closed one half of the folding doors, and, holding the other ajar, called out to the little Pole:
"Most illustrious, will you kindly withdraw as well?"
"My dear Dmitri Fyodorovitch," said Trifon Borissovitch, "make them give you back what you lost. It's as good as stolen from you."
"I don't want my fifty roubles back," Kalganov declared suddenly.
"I don't want my two hundred either," cried Mitya, "I wouldn't take it for anything! Let him keep it as a consolation."
"Bravo, Mitya! You're a trump, Mitya!" cried Grushenka, and there was a note of fierce anger in the exclamation.
The little pan, crimson with rage but still mindful of his dignity, was heading for the door, but stopped short and turned suddenly to Grushenka:
"Pani, if you want to come with me, come. If not, farewell."

And swelling with indignation and self-importance, he went to the door. Here was a man of real character: he thought so well of himself that even after all that had happened, he still expected she would marry him. Mitya slammed the door behind him.
"Lock it," said Kalganov. But the key clicked from the other side — they'd already locked it from within.
"That's perfect!" Grushenka exclaimed, without mercy. "Serves them right!"
